title: How the 1982–83 El Niño developed
description: Evidence-based reconstruction of the 1982–83 El Niño: preconditions, triggers, amplifiers and the broader climate system, with timeline, evidence table and verified references.
lit_cutoff: open, updated as new studies appear
status_note: Stages 1–3 of 5 complete, with added assessments of the MJO, documented 1982 westerly bursts, El Chichón and Indian–Pacific interactions, and a citation audit (18 Oct 2026). Sources verified (DOIs checked against Crossref; what was read is stated for each reference), monthly data assembled, timeline and evidence table drafted. Prose sections are not written yet; they follow your review of this evidence. Items marked Pending still need event-specific evidence.

sections.title: Scope, index and data
sections.html:
This page holds the evidence assembled so far (stages 1–3 of 5). The paper's prose will be drafted from it after review. Primary index: NOAA's Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), official since 1 February 2026 [18] [14]: the three-month mean of Niño 3.4 minus the 20°N–20°S tropical-mean anomaly, rescaled. On RONI the 1982–83 peak is +2.40 (DJF 1983), the strongest of the three historical events in this series; on the traditional ONI it is +2.14.

Observing system in 1982. No TAO mooring array (completed in 1994), no satellite altimetry (from 1992) and no Argo floats. The evidence rests on ship and XBT tracks, island tide gauges, a few moorings (e.g. 0°, 110°W) and later reanalyses. Satellite SST from April 1982 was biased low by up to 2.5 °C by El Chichón aerosol [1]. Subsurface indices for 1981–82 are reconstructions from sparse data.

sections.title: Monthly indices, Jan 1981 – Jun 1983
sections.html: Values from NOAA CPC and PMEL files as held in the site's data archive; read from the source files, not retyped.

table.note: RONI and ONI are three-month means centred on the month. SOI and trade-wind indices are standardized (negative SOI and negative trade anomalies are El Niño-like). OLR in W m⁻² (negative = more convection). Heat content in °C vs 1981–2010; WWV in 10¹⁴ m³; DMI in °C. OISST begins Sep 1981 and its 1982 values may carry residual El Chichón bias.

timeline: Warm water volume (WWV) positive all year, +0.6 to +2.1 × 10¹⁴ m³; upper-300 m heat content (180°–100°W) between −0.7 and +1.0 °C.
Recharge of the equatorial warm-water reservoir, the precondition in recharge-oscillator theory.

Strong, coherent MJO: OMI amplitude ≥ 1 from 25 Nov to 21 Jan (max 2.3); 20–100-day convection moves from 105°E (26 Nov) to 155°E (14–17 Dec) with 850 hPa westerlies behind it; also seen in FMO, VPM and the ENSO-filtered RMM* (max 1.7). Weickmann reports interannual transitions in Sep 1981–Apr 1982 coinciding with strong MJO passages into the Pacific.
Intraseasonal westerly forcing in the western Pacific during the transition phase (association, not isolated as a cause).
850 hPa trades weaker than normal in the western Pacific (−0.6 to −1.3 standardized); heat content rises to +0.9 °C. Niño 1+2 cold (−0.72 to −1.38 °C, OISST).
Early westerly anomalies in the west; coastal coolness consistent with enhanced south-east Pacific trades in the post-1976 background state.
Reanalysis westerly burst: 1000 hPa anomaly up to +12 m s⁻¹ at 147.5°–165°E (NCEP/NCAR R1, 5°S–5°N). MJO only marginal (OMI phase 6, amplitude 1.0–1.4 for about a week). No published account found.
Possible early Kelvin-wave forcing; ocean response not documented.

El Chichón eruptions (Mexico) inject aerosol into the tropical stratosphere. Just before them (March) the warm water volume anomaly is +2.15 × 10¹⁴ m³, the 96th percentile of 1980–2025 months, and heat content is +0.9 °C. Satellite (AVHRR) SST biased low by up to 2.5 °C for months.
Pre-existing recharge; candidate volcanic forcing evaluated separately below. Certainly an observing-system problem for satellite SST.

Westerly wind burst documented from 12-hourly island, atoll and ship reports: 11 days, within about 5° of the equator, growing from about 1000 km to over 3500 km in zonal extent; strongest over 135°–155°E. OLR-based indices show an active MJO (OMI phases 6–7, up to 2.3; convection at 80°E on 21–27 Apr, then 150°E by 9 May), but BoM RMM is only 0.6–1.2 during the burst.

Authors attribute the burst to a midlatitude-forced pressure rise in the far western equatorial Pacific, prolonged by a pressure fall near 150°–160°E; they describe it as the first sustained burst of 1982, about three months before onset.
ERSSTv6 relative Niño 3.4 rises from +0.76 to +1.12 °C; SOI −1.0 by June; RONI MAM +0.46 → AMJ +0.74.
Band of anomalous southerly winds east of Australia (150°–160°E) crosses the equator just before sustained westerlies appear on the equator west of the Date Line.
Cross-equatorial flow feeding sustained equatorial westerlies that force downwelling Kelvin waves.
Strong anomalous warming starts along the equator, before the South American coast warms.
Kelvin-wave-induced eastward currents advect warm water while the seasonal east–west SST gradient is strong; reproduced by an advective and a full ocean model.
Equatorial Undercurrent at 159°W decays; near-surface flow at 0°, 110°W reverses to eastward; central-Pacific OLR −21 W m⁻².
Basin-wide adjustment of the sea-surface slope to westerly forcing; deep convection moving east.
Undercurrent partly reversed at 159°W; central Pacific trades −2.0 standardized; RONI JAS +1.14.
Bjerknes feedback: warming weakens trades, which deepen the thermocline in the east.

SST in the equatorial zone of the eastern tropical Pacific 5 °C above the long-term monthly mean; Galápagos sea level +22 cm; thermocline 50–70 m deeper along the equator and the South American coast.
Consistent with downwelling Kelvin waves and coupled growth (interpretation; see the Kelvin-wave row of the evidence table).
Reanalysis westerly burst, peak +9.4 m s⁻¹ on 30 Aug at 162.5°–185°E; convection moved from 65°–70°E (2–8 Aug) to 175°–180°E (29 Aug–1 Sep), but the circulation test failed and RMM was 0.5–1.0.
Burst during the growth phase (RONI JAS +1.14); not supported as MJO-organised.

Coupled positive Indian Ocean Dipole: DMI peaks in October (+1.04 °C ERSSTv5; CPC +0.92 °C) with equatorial Indian Ocean surface easterly anomalies of −2.5 to −3.1 m s⁻¹ (Oct–Nov). The eastern-pole cooling had begun in January–February, but without sustained easterlies until July–August.
Its SON size matches what Niño 3.4 alone predicts (see Indian–Pacific section); model studies suggest it may in turn have intensified the eastern-Pacific warming.
First Galápagos sea-level peak; warm water drains from north of the equator; by year-end the normal east–west sea-level slope is gone. WWV falls to +1.4 × 10¹⁴ m³.
Discharge of the warm-water reservoir driven by western Pacific westerlies.
Peak: RONI +2.40 (ONI +2.14). January SOI −3.5; central-Pacific OLR −46 W m⁻²; WWV negative.
Mature, fully coupled state; discharge under way.
Western Pacific surface winds turn to easterly anomalies (−1.0 to −1.6 m s⁻¹, 130°–160°E); tropical Indian Ocean basin-wide warm (+0.1 to +0.2 °C, 40°–100°E, 20°S–20°N).
One modelled pathway by which basin-wide Indian Ocean warming hastens the end of El Niño.
Recovery of the zonal pressure gradient in the central Pacific.
Niño 3.4 declines while Niño 1+2 rises to +4.0 °C in June; second Galápagos sea-level peak in May as warm water drains from south of the equator.
A second, southern-hemisphere draining episode prolongs warmth in the far east.
Sea level below normal across the equatorial Pacific.
Warm water lost to higher latitudes: the end of the cycle.
evidence: WWV positive through 1981 and early 1982; heat content rising from Jan 1982.
A deep, charged warm pool lets Kelvin waves raise eastern SST and sustain growth.
Sustained equatorial westerlies west of the Date Line (from Jun 1982)
Appear in June; later extend east and persist.
Wind forcing of downwelling Kelvin waves and eastward currents.
Trigger of the vigorous phase, then amplifier
Cross-equatorial southerly jet east of Australia (Jun 1982)
Formed just before the sustained westerlies.
B/C: one event-specific study; similar precursors in 1957, 1965, 1972
Downwelling Kelvin waves and anomalous eastward advection
Equatorial warming from July; undercurrent collapse Aug–Sep; thermocline 50–70 m deeper by Oct.
Eastward transfer of warm water and anomalous advection.
A−: event observations + advective and full ocean model experiments
Seasonal timing (annual cycle of the zonal SST gradient)
Westerly-driven currents arrived mid-year rather than in Feb–Apr.
The same currents give equatorial-first warming when the zonal SST gradient is strong.
B: model experiment for this event
Tropical Pacific warmer after the late 1970s; south-east Pacific trades enhanced at onset; coast cold in early 1982.
Background state alters the onset cyclone and makes coastal warming follow, not lead, central warming.
Trades, SOI, OLR and SST strengthen together from Aug to Dec 1982.
Warming → weaker trades → deeper eastern thermocline → more warming.
B: event observations (CPC indices) + general theory
Recharge–discharge and the second eastern peak
WWV discharged by Jan 1983; two draining episodes (north then south of the equator).
Discharge ends the event; southern draining prolongs far-eastern warmth to mid-1983.
A−: sea-level budget for this event
No twin tropical cyclogenesis in the JTWC best tracks during the 1982–83 El Niño under either the Keen or the Harrison–Giese definition (1969–2006 survey).
Cyclone pairs straddling the equator produce brief strong westerlies (shown for 1971–79).

Island records show the central-Pacific easterlies weakened before each El Niño of 1950–78 except 1963, through bursts of 1–3 weeks (general mechanism, not 1982). For 1982: a documented 11-day burst on 6–16 May; sustained westerlies from June; a succession of westerly pulses to November (cited by Chu and Frederick). Reanalysis adds bursts on 28 Mar–3 Apr and 24 Aug–3 Sep. A complete 1982 episode catalogue has not yet been assembled in this review.
Bursts force downwelling Kelvin waves; the ocean response to individual 1982 bursts is not isolated in the sources read.
B for the May wind event; C for its contribution

MJO-like activity in Dec 1981 (all five indices) and late Mar 1982 (strict propagation test passed); late Apr–May 1982 MJO-like in OLR-based indices but marginal in RMM during the May burst. A conference reconstruction places Kelvin waves after MJO convection in Apr, May–Jun and Nov 1982. From Oct 1982 MJO convection reached 155°–170°W and Indian Ocean–Maritime Continent intraseasonal OLR variance was the second lowest of 1979–2001.
MJO westerlies can force Kelvin waves; conversely El Niño shifts MJO activity east (ENSO influence on the MJO).
Contribution to onset unresolved; late-1982 changes partly a consequence
C: event-specific association; no peer-reviewed study isolates the MJO's ocean effect in 1982

Erupted 29 Mar–4 Apr 1982, after recharge (WWV 96th percentile) and after western-Pacific trade weakening and the Dec 1981 MJO; the 28 Mar–3 Apr reanalysis burst began the day before the first eruption.
Proposed pathways act through land cooling and drying months later.
Initiation not supported by the timing; unresolved
D: no study isolates the observed onset
Maritime Continent drying and enhanced western-Pacific MJO activity in Jul–Nov 1982 (observed composite with Pinatubo).

Land drying → MJO propagation → more bursts (CESM2); African or South–Southeast Asian drying → westerlies (other models). Pathways and magnitudes differ between models, and the observed signals are also typical El Niño responses.
C: model studies; observations cannot separate forcing from internal variability
[41] [43] [13] [44] [42] [4]
SE tropical Indian Ocean −0.3 to −0.5 °C from Feb, before Niño 3.4 warmed; no sustained equatorial easterlies until Jul–Aug.
Not the Indian Ocean Bjerknes feedback at this stage; origin not established.
Indian Ocean: Pacific forcing of the IOD (Sep–Nov 1982)
Coupled positive IOD after Niño 3.4 exceeded +1.3 °C; SON DMI +0.58 °C against +0.61 °C expected from Niño 3.4 (1950–2024 regression).
Eastward shift of Walker circulation → easterlies over the eastern Indian Ocean.
Indian Ocean: feedback on Pacific growth and peak

Forecast runs without Indian Ocean coupling underestimate the 1982–83 peak (the model also over-predicted the 1982 IOD); a simple model forced with IOD-induced winds reproduces eastern-Pacific intensification of 1972, 1982 and 1997; decoupled hindcasts weaken super El Niños. One CGCM finds no significant Pacific impact from a fall IOD.
IOD-induced westerly anomalies over the Pacific strengthen eastern warming.
Basin-wide warming Dec 1982–Jul 1983; western Pacific easterly anomalies Dec–Apr; a second positive DMI in Jun–Aug 1983; NDJ 1983–84 Niño 3.4 −0.8 °C (detrended ERSSTv5).
Basin warming strengthens western-Pacific easterlies; a positive IOD favours La Niña the following year.
Usually a lagged response to El Niño.

after.title: What is not yet established
after.html:
• Westerly bursts. A complete 1982 episode catalogue has not yet been assembled in this review; Chu (1989), Sumathipala (1989) and Sadler (1983) remain to be retrieved, and the reanalysis burst list should be checked against JRA-55 or ERA5.
  • MJO, El Chichón and the Indian Ocean. Assessed above; all three contributions remain unresolved or model-dependent.
  • Full texts. Gill & Rasmusson (1983) could not be read at all; for the 1983 Science papers only abstracts were read (see the citation audit).
  • What was knowable at the time. The 1982 event was compared with a six-event composite [20] and departed markedly from the usual pattern [19] [2]; coupled-model forecasts began only with the 1986 event [3].

post_sections.title: MJO contribution (assessment)
post_sections.html:
Answer so far. Several diagnostics, together with daily-field inspection, support identifying the December 1981 and late March 1982 episodes as MJO-like intraseasonal activity, and the late April–May 1982 sequence as MJO-like in OLR-based measures. Whether any of these episodes triggered or amplified the El Niño is unresolved (grade C): that needs evidence linking their wind forcing to the ocean response, and the one reconstruction that does so is so far available only as a conference abstract. From late 1982 the MJO was itself altered by El Niño, so the interaction ran both ways.

Event-specific literature.

  • Weickmann (1991), abstract only: six MJOs in September 1981–April 1982, with interannual transitions coinciding with strong MJO passages into the Pacific [27].
  • Li et al. (2023), full text: an ERA-Interim and BoM RMM analysis of the three super El Niños [53]. It finds eastward-propagating MJO activity in the developing stage (February–September) of all three, but the weakest eastward power in 1982/83 (main period about 40 days). It reports two prominent eastward propagations of MJO westerlies in that stage. In their Figure 2A, RMM exceeds 1.2 in early April and late May–early June 1982. The authors note that the MJO's role in 1982 "had not been deeply examined due to the lack of data". They link the weak, eastward-shifted mature-stage MJO to El Niño-driven circulation and moisture anomalies, and warn that RMM and zonal-wind amplitude can give contradictory results.
  • Roundy and Kiladis, 87th AMS Annual Meeting extended abstract (paper 5B.4, 2007), full text: Kelvin-wave dynamic height reconstructed from island sea levels and OLR, trained on TAO. Besides the December 1981 Kelvin wave, it finds intraseasonal Kelvin waves in March–April, June–July and November 1982, and eastward-moving MJO convection preceding wave development in April, May–June and November [54]. This is a research lead, not peer-reviewed evidence. The related journal paper (Roundy and Kiladis 2007, J. Climate 20, 4341–4355) has not yet been read [55]. Their 2006 journal paper, read as the author's manuscript, covers 1988–2005 only [56].
  • Chu and Frederick (1990) document the May 1982 burst and attribute its origin to midlatitude pressure forcing; they do not discuss the MJO [28].

Published indices: what was available for each episode. All five files were retrieved on 18 October 2026.

table.note: The indices are not independent: OMI, FMO, RMM and RMM* all use NOAA interpolated OLR; RMM, RMM* and VPM use NCEP winds; and our diagnostics below reuse the same interpolated OLR and NCEP/NCAR R1 winds. Agreement between them is useful but is not independent validation. VPM phase numbers are not used because its sign convention was not verified.

post_sections.html_after:
Our three diagnostics (documented; not validated MJO indices). Code: tools/papers/mjo_1982_diag.py; outputs in data/papers/1982/.

  • Data. NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 daily u at 850, 200 and 1000 hPa (2.5° grid) and NOAA interpolated daily OLR, 1979–2001, via PSL THREDDS [39] [61].
  • Averaging. Cosine-weighted mean over 10°S–10°N (1000 hPa: 5°S–5°N), giving one value per 2.5° of longitude.
  • Anomalies. Departures from a 1979–2000 climatology: the mean plus the first three annual harmonics, fitted by least squares.
  • D1 (Wheeler–Hendon style). Subtract the mean of the previous 120 days. Scale each field by its standard deviation over all longitudes and days. Run a combined EOF (SVD) of OLR, u850 and u200 over 1979–2001. Scale the first two principal components to unit variance, and set the sign of PC2 so that PC1 leads it at a 10-day lag. Amplitude = √(PC1² + PC2²). No ENSO regression is removed, unlike BoM RMM. The two EOFs explain 13.0% and 11.2% of variance.
  • D2 (band-pass). As D1, but the anomalies are FFT band-passed to 20–100 days instead of removing the 120-day mean (21.1% and 19.8%).
  • D3 (OLR only). EOFs of band-passed OLR alone (24.6% and 17.1%).
  • Bursts. Unfiltered 1000 hPa anomaly ≥ 5 m s⁻¹ for ≥ 3 days over ≥ 10° of longitude within 120°E–150°W.

Propagation test. Code: tools/papers/mjo_1982_tests.py. All four parts use the 20–100-day fields at 10°S–10°N:

  1. T1. Indian Ocean convection: OLR ≤ −15 W m⁻² somewhere in 70°–100°E.
  2. T2. Western-Pacific convection: OLR ≤ −15 W m⁻² in 140°E–180°, 8–35 days after T1. Over the ~65° between the boxes this means 2.4–10.4 m s⁻¹, bracketing the typical ~5 m s⁻¹ [57].
  3. T3. Lag-correlation speed: correlate OLR at 60°E–180° with the 70°–100°E mean at lags of −5 to +35 days. Fitting the best lag at each longitude (r ≥ 0.4) must give 2–10 m s⁻¹ eastward.
  4. T4. Circulation: within ±2 days of the western-Pacific convection, u850 over the 30° west of its centre is westerly and u200 easterly on at least 3 of 5 days.

A first version that tracked the single daily OLR minimum failed every window, because the minimum jumps between systems and convection weakens over the Maritime Continent; it was replaced before results were interpreted.

Base rates. In sliding 45-day windows from January 1981 to May 1983, T1 + T2 + T4 hold in 55% of windows and all four tests in 19%. Passing T1, T2 and T4 alone is therefore weak evidence; we treat all four as the strict test.

post_sections.html_after:
What this supports. Multiple diagnostics and the daily fields support identifying the December 1981 and late March 1982 episodes, and the late April–May 1982 sequence in OLR-based measures, as MJO-like intraseasonal activity. The episodes match the months in which Roundy and Kiladis reconstruct Kelvin waves (March–April, May–June and November 1982), but that link rests on a conference abstract until their 2007 journal paper is read. The stronger claim — that an MJO episode triggered or amplified the 1982 El Niño — still requires evidence connecting its wind forcing to the subsequent ocean response. Ocean-model studies show that MJO winds can force Kelvin waves and rectify into low-frequency SST anomalies [59] [60], and Kelvin-wave forcing by the MJO preceded larger eastern-Pacific SST anomalies in 1980–99 warm events [35]; none of these isolates the effect in 1982.

Two-way interaction. From October 1982 MJO convection reached 170°–155°W, and October–March intraseasonal OLR variance over 60°–150°E was the second lowest of 22 seasons (1979–2001; only 1997–98 was lower). This matches the eastward shift and reduced activity reported for exceptional warm events [33] [34], and Li et al.'s finding that El Niño-driven circulation and moisture changes altered the mature-stage MJO in 1982/83 [53]. These features are a consequence of El Niño, not evidence that the MJO drove it.

Bursts and base rate. By the burst definition above, 1982 had 13 bursts against a 1979–2001 mean of 4.4 a year (range 0–16; 1997 had 16). Part of the late-1982 count reflects the El Niño's own slow westerly anomaly. Most bursts in 1979–2002 were tied to MJO-like convection, but MJO amplitude itself was not correlated with burst frequency [36].

Next steps. Read Roundy and Kiladis (2007, J. Climate); test the windows with a second reanalysis (JRA-55 or ERA5); and look for an ocean-model hindcast of 1982 forced with and without intraseasonal winds.

That supports the general mechanism; it does not document the 1982 episodes. The May 1982 study cited in the Vecchi–Harrison atlas is Chu and Frederick (1990) [30] [28]. For each documented episode the table separates the wind event, its atmospheric origin, the ocean response and its contribution. Observing a burst does not by itself raise the causal grade.

post_sections.title: El Chichón as an external forcing (assessment)
post_sections.html:
Initiation and subsequent growth are judged separately.

Initiation: not supported by the timing; formally unresolved. The eruptions were on 29 March and 3–4 April 1982 [45]. Before them the equatorial Pacific was already recharged — warm water volume +2.15 × 10¹⁴ m³ in March, the 96th percentile of 1980–2025 months — and western-Pacific trades were already weaker than normal (Feb–Apr), after the strong December 1981 MJO [62] [27]. Khodri et al. note that ocean reanalyses show high equatorial heat content before El Chichón, and that a warm event was already under way during two of the four large historical eruptions they list (Santa María 1902, Agung 1963, El Chichón 1982, Pinatubo 1991), without naming which two [13]. In GFDL CM2.1 ensembles the ENSO response depends on the ocean state and timing, and when a strong El Niño is already developing at an April eruption the volcanic effect is unlikely to be visible [42]. With only three observed cases, Chai et al. state that the westerlies after Agung, El Chichón and Pinatubo cannot be attributed to the eruptions rather than internal variability [43]. Robock et al. (1995) are reported by later papers to have concluded that the 1982 event began before the eruption; that paper was not read, so this is indirect evidence [46].

Growth: possible weak amplifier, unresolved. Several models produce westerly anomalies over the western-central Pacific within months of a tropical eruption — through tropical African cooling and a Kelvin-wave response [13], through South–Southeast Asian and West African drying (8 of 11 models) [43], or through Maritime Continent cooling [44]. Kim et al. propose that faster land drying around the warm pool helps the MJO propagate into the western Pacific, raising burst frequency (by about 76% in CESM2) and the chance of El Niño onset [41]. For 1982 that pathway bears on growth rather than onset: their observed signals are in July–November 1982, after the documented May burst and the June westerlies; Maritime Continent drying and enhanced central-Pacific MJO activity are also normal El Niño responses; the ensemble was screened on an April–June recharge index that includes post-eruption months (0.9σ in 1982, which the authors class as neutral); and HadGEM3 did not reproduce the result. Proxy records show no consistent ENSO response to eruptions over the last millennium [4].

Observing-system effect (certain). Volcanic aerosol biased satellite SST low by up to 2.5 °C [1]. A reprocessed OSTIA record found unexplained biases in May and Oct–Dec 1982 in its single AVHRR input, which the authors attribute mainly to instrument calibration rather than the eruption [45]. RONI and ONI use the in-situ ERSST record.

post_sections.html_after:
Statistics (base rates and lead–lag). DMI and Niño 3.4 in SON correlate at r = 0.59 (n = 75). Regressing SON DMI on SON Niño 3.4 (excluding 1982) predicts +0.61 °C for 1982; the observed value was +0.58 °C (residual 0.07 standard deviations). By this measure the 1982 IOD was as large as ENSO alone would make it. The JJA DMI adds no information about NDJ Niño 3.4 once JJA Niño 3.4 is known (partial r = 0.02). The SON DMI is negatively related to the following year's NDJ Niño 3.4 after removing SON Niño 3.4 (partial r = −0.30), in line with the reported tendency for a positive IOD to be followed by La Niña [52]. Of 17 years with SON DMI above +0.4 °C (1950–2024), 11 coincided with El Niño.

Initiation. No evidence that the Indian Ocean initiated the event. The early eastern-pole cooling preceded Pacific warming but lacked the wind feedback, and no study tests it for 1982.

Growth and peak. Pacific forcing of the IOD is well supported: the El Niño-related loss of Maritime Continent convection drives easterlies over the eastern Indian Ocean [50]. Feedback the other way is supported only by models that include 1982: forecasts with Indian Ocean coupling suppressed underestimate the 1982–83 peak, though that model over-predicted the 1982 IOD [47]; a simple model driven by IOD-induced winds (heating taken from the 1982 and 1997 OLR composites) reproduces eastern-Pacific intensification [48]; decoupling the Indian and Atlantic Oceans weakens super El Niños, with coupling between the two oceans the key factor [49]. Against this, one coupled model found no significant Pacific impact from a fall IOD [51], and a pIOD can also favour La Niña-like conditions when the Seychelles–Chagos ridge warms [50]. Verdict: plausible amplifier of the late-1982 growth and peak, model-dependent (grade C).

Persistence and decay. In one coupled model, basin-wide Indian Ocean warming in DJF strengthens western-Pacific easterlies and hastens the El Niño–La Niña transition [51]. The observed 1983 sequence (basin warming, western-Pacific easterlies, then the weak 1983–84 La Niña) is consistent with that, but not tested for 1983 specifically (grade C).
